---
title: "Predictive modeling of claims status"
author: 'Phillip, Caroline, Aileen, Tyler'
date: today
---

### Abstract

The text from page titles, meta descriptions, headers, and paragraphs was scraped from the raw HTML webpages, depending on the model. They were cleaned and converted into TF-IDF weights of word tokens. For the binary classification, an elastic-net logistic regression achieved an estimated 80% accuracy (AUC about 0.87). For multiclass classification, a linear support vector machine achieved an estimated 83.9% accuracy. Both estimates come from held-out portions of the labeled data.

### Preprocessing

For the binary classification, text was extracted from headers (h1 to h4) and paragraphs. We then removed the URLs, emails, punctuation, digits, and symbols and text was lowercased, stripped of stop words, and lemmatized. The pages were then represented by TF-IDF weights. The binary model used single words appearing on at least 5 training pages. Vocabulary and IDF weights were learned from training pages only and reused on test pages. Pages with no usable text (about 4% of the test set) received a default label.

For the multi-class classification, we extracted the title, meta description, and paragraph text from the HTML. We followed the same cleaning steps as the binary classification. We applied unigram tokenization for title and meta description. Paragraph text got both unigram and bigram tokenization. Tokens are prefixed by field, so a title word and a paragraph word are different features. We represented the cleaned text with TF-IDF over terms that occur at least 3 times, capped at the 10,000 most frequent.

### Methods

For the binary classification, an elastic-net logistic regression (glmnet) was fit to the TF-IDF features. The mixing parameter was chosen from {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1} by validation AUC, and ridge (0) was selected. The penalty strength was chosen by 10-fold cross-validation. The pages with no usable text were labeled as “N/A,” which is the most common label among such pages in the training data. The final model was refit on all labeled pages.

For the multi-class classification, we went with a linear SVM (one-vs-rest), tuning the cost parameter with 5-fold stratified CV. The best model was selected based on accuracy. The train-test split was 80/20 stratified split. The final model was trained on the 80% training split.The same fallback of "N/A" was also used.

### Results

The binary model reached about 80% accuracy (AUC about 0.87) on a held-out 20% of the labeled pages. Accuracy was nearly identical across all alpha values (79.9% to 80.6%). The multi-class model reached about 83.9% accuracy on its own held-out 20%. Each estimate comes from a single split, so each carries a margin of roughly 2 percentage points. The two models used different preprocessing and different splits, so the numbers are not directly comparable.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
library(knitr)
bin_tbl <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Accuracy", "Sensitivity", "Specificity"),
  `Value (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", c(80.4, 82.2, 78.0)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(bin_tbl, align = c("l", "r"),
      caption = "Binary test-set performance")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
summary_tbl <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("Accuracy",
             "Sensitivity (macro-averaged)",
             "Specificity (macro-averaged)"),
  `Value (%)` = sprintf("%.1f", c(83.9, 74.6, 95.0)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(summary_tbl, align = c("l", "r"),
      caption = "Multiclass test-set performance")
```
